name: Billiard
lede: Billiard is the deep green of the cloth on a billiard table, a color that arrived in the Maerz & Paul dictionary in 1930 and carries a surprisingly large share of the story of how people feel about green.

sections.title: The cloth
sections.body:
Billiard, or billiard green, names the deep green of the baize on billiard and snooker tables [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists it on plate 29, with a first recorded use in 1920 [2]. The swatch here is a dark, muted green, close to [[hunter-green]], with [[racing-green]] and [[bottle-green]] among the same family of deep greens [2][1].

Pastoureau treats the table as one case of a wider rule: green is the color of games and gaming, and he points to billiards, played on green felt, as proof [3]. Cards and indoor sports follow the same habit [3].

sections.title: The table that went purple
sections.body:
In 1934 Faber Birren set up as a color consultant in Chicago, and his first real break came from a billiard-table maker, the Brunswick-Balke-Collender Company [4]. Home buyers were not buying tables for basement game rooms [4]. Birren found that American women disliked green tops because they linked the color with cheap pool halls and gambling dens [4]. He advised a soft purplish covering instead, the company went along, and sales of the purple-topped models for the home rose fast [4].

This is Birren's own account, in the introduction to his book, and no second source in the books confirms the sales figures [4]. It remains a neat case of a color's reputation outweighing its function.

sections.title: Van Gogh's table
sections.body: The most famous painted billiard table is in Van Gogh's *The Night Café*, which he described to his brother in 1888 [3][5]. He wrote that he had tried to express terrible human passions with red and green, setting a green table against a blood-red room [3][5]. Translators disagree on the table's color, rendering it as green or yellow-green, and the same letter calls the walls dull or dark yellow in different editions [3][5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive, a color within six units of this swatch fills at least five per cent of the canvas in 39 of 23,781 paintings [6]. Dennis Miller Bunker's [[painting:nga-103247|Roadside Cottage]] of 1889 holds it across 46 per cent of the picture, and Klimt's [[painting:commons-Q19883563|The Park]] of 1909 across 42 per cent [6]. The match rate rises sharply in the 1900s, 14 hits among 1,674 paintings, against 19 among 8,345 in the 1800s [6].

Paintings that carry billiard share their canvas most often with Hunter green, 37 of the 39 times [6]. The color sits in the shadow range of its paintings in about two cases in three [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match shows a screen color near this one, not a pigment [6].

choices: Buyers linked green tops with pool halls and gambling dens
